messages.author: 15280b836cfcd1eb
messages.subject: Off.set term for DSM predictions
parts:
Hello, 

I am using the DSM package for the first time and using Dave Miller's vignette as a guide.  My question is whether the off.set parameter for predictions should be the effective area searched (or the effective half area) or whether it should be the size of the cell that I want predictions for (as implied by the vignette).  I want my predictions to be in terms of density (animals per km^2) at each of my prediction points, so I used offset = 1000*1000.  Is this correct?

Non-reproducible example code:

# Estimating the detection function with BF as a covariate
ds.model <- ds(flatfile, adjustment="cos", order=2, formula=~as.factor(BFDummy))

# Fitting a DSM model with a spline on latitude and longitude and yearday as a covariate
dsm.model <- dsm(Nhat~s(X,Y, k=30) + factor(YDay), 
                 ds.model$ddf, seg.data, obs.data, family=Tweedie(p=1.20), 
                 method="REML")

# Density predictions at each of the prediction points
predictions$DSM <- predict(dsm.model, predictions, off.set=1000*1000)

Thanks for your help!

Eiren

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Off.set term for DSM predictions
parts:
Eiren:

The offset is used in conjunction with the function predict().  As a consequence, the value you specify for the offset is the size of your **prediction grid**.  You will have values everywhere throughout your study area for the predictors from which you constructed your density surface model.  In the example you provided, your predictors are X, Y and yearday.  Yearday will be the same throughout your prediction grid, but X and Y take on values dependent upon location within the prediction grid.  The size of the prediction grid cells are what you specify for the offset.

Hope that is helpful.

  c(288,290,304),

names(pred) <- c("YDay", "X", "Y")

model.predict <- predict(dsm.model, pred, off.set=(.25*1000*1000))

I believe that the model.predict output is therefore in units of animals per .25 km^2 within each grid cell.

But I also need density estimates in terms of animals/km^2 at a handful of specific X, Y locations on each of three yeardays, so I used:

Where predictions contains X, Y and YDay values for 10 locations on three days.  Am I correct that given an off.set of 1000*1000, the predict function will return density in animals per km^2 at each of those locations on each of the days?

parts:
Eiren:

Think you may have stumbled at the first hurdle.  If your grid cells are 250m (0.25km) on a side, then the area of the cell is 0.25^2=0.0625km^2

The offset you provide is simply to convert density into abundance.  If all you wish to report is density, and not abundance, you need not specify an offset.

messages.author: 15280b836cfcd1eb
messages.subject: Re: Off.set term for DSM predictions
parts:
Hello All, 

With Eric's help, I was able to clarify that the off.set parameter when using the predict() function should be the size of the prediction grid cell (in units consistent with the spatial terms in the DSM; for me, this was meters).  The predict function will return the number of animals in each cell.  So, in my case,
predictions$DSM <- predict(dsm.model, predictions, off.set=1000*1000)

would return values of animals per km^2, which was my goal.  Alternatively, specifying off.set=1 would return density in animals per m^2, which could then be converted to animals per km^2.

Thanks!

Eiren
